overview.title: Preparing the next model generation and chapter 6 summary
overview.chapter: 6 The universal workflow of machine learning
overview.main_topic: The last maintenance advice (watch production data, keep annotating, focus on hard samples), the authors' closing remarks on the big picture, and the chapter summary of the three-phase universal workflow.
overview.central_idea: Prepare the replacement model as soon as the current one launches: watch for new features and label changes, and keep collecting data, especially hard examples. Model development is only one of three phases (define the task, develop a model, deploy) that make up every ML project.
overview.importance: This page condenses the whole chapter into a reusable checklist. The rest of the book focuses on model development, and this summary places that work inside the full workflow.
learning_objectives: Name the two ways to prepare the next generation of a deployed model
Explain why hard-to-classify samples are especially valuable to collect
Recall the steps of each phase of the universal workflow: define, develop, deploy
Explain why model development is only one part of an ML project
prerequisites: Concept drift and model lifespans (p.212, p.201)
The chapter 6 sections on task definition (p.196–p.202), model development (p.203–p.207) and deployment (p.207–p.212)
Evaluation protocols: hold-out and K-fold validation (chapter 5)

summary:
The page finishes section **6.3.4 Maintaining your model**. As soon as a model launches, you should start getting ready to train the **next generation** that will replace it:

- **Watch for changes in production data.** Are new features becoming available? Should the label set be expanded or edited?
- **Keep collecting and annotating data**, and keep improving the annotation pipeline. Pay special attention to **samples that seem difficult for the current model**, because they are the most likely to improve performance.

The authors then close the **universal workflow of machine learning**. It is a lot to keep in mind, and expertise takes time, but the reader now sees the *entire spectrum* of an ML project. Most of the book focuses on model development, which is only one part of the workflow: "Always keep in mind the big picture!"

The **chapter summary** restates the workflow in three phases:

1. **Define the problem**: understand the broader context (end goal, constraints); collect and annotate a dataset and understand it in depth; choose how to measure success and which metrics to monitor on validation data.
2. **Develop a model**: prepare the data; pick an evaluation protocol (hold-out or K-fold, and which portion to use for validation); achieve statistical power by beating a simple baseline; scale up to a model that can overfit; then regularize and tune hyperparameters using validation performance. The authors note that a lot of ML research focuses only on this last step.
3. **Deploy** once the model performs well on the test data: set appropriate expectations with stakeholders; optimize a final model for inference and ship it to the chosen environment (web server, mobile, browser, embedded device, etc.); monitor production performance and keep collecting data for the next generation.

The last step leads back to the first, so the workflow forms a loop.

paragraphs.excerpt: As soon as your model has launched, you should be getting ready
paragraphs.what_it_says: Once the model launches, start preparing the next generation that will replace it.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Because of concept drift (p.212), replacement is certain. The only question is when, so preparation should start at launch rather than when performance collapses.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It turns maintenance into planned, continuous work rather than firefighting.

terminology.meaning: A version of a production model; each new generation is trained on newer data and replaces the previous one.

connections: p.212: no model lasts forever; lifespans of days to years

paragraphs.excerpt: Watch out for changes in the production data. Are new features
paragraphs.what_it_says: Watch for changes in production data: new features becoming available, and whether the label set should be expanded or edited.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The problem itself can change, not just the data distribution. New input signals may appear (e.g., new user metadata), and new categories may be needed (e.g., a new type of spam).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The next generation may need a different input schema or output head, not only retraining on fresh data.

terminology.meaning: The set of target classes the model predicts.

connections: p.198: collecting a dataset and defining annotations

paragraphs.excerpt: Keep collecting and annotating data, and keep improving your annotation pipeline over
paragraphs.what_it_says: Keep collecting and annotating data and improving the annotation pipeline. Focus on samples that seem hard for the current model, which are most likely to improve performance.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Hard samples, such as low-confidence predictions or errors found in audits, carry the most new information. Easy samples the model already handles add little.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It makes labeling budgets go much further. Beyond the book, this idea is formalized as active learning and hard-example mining.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: a simple selection rule is uncertainty sampling, e.g., pick production inputs whose top softmax probability is below a threshold for human annotation.

terminology.meaning: The tools and people that turn raw data into labeled training examples.

connections: p.212: manual audits reuse the annotation infrastructure
p.199: annotation for the cookie project

paragraphs.excerpt: This concludes the universal workflow of machine learning—that’s a lot of things
paragraphs.what_it_says: This ends the universal workflow. Expertise takes time, but the reader now knows the full spectrum of an ML project. The rest of the book focuses mostly on model development, which is only one part of the workflow, so keep the big picture in mind.
paragraphs.what_it_means: It is a reminder that the architectures and techniques in later chapters all sit inside the define–develop–deploy loop.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It guards against the common habit of optimizing models without regard for the problem definition, data quality or deployment constraints.

terminology.meaning: The book's general three-phase blueprint for any ML project: define the task, develop a model, deploy it.

paragraphs.excerpt: When you take on a new machine learning project, first, define the
paragraphs.what_it_says: Summary, phase 1: define the problem. Understand the broader context (end goal and constraints), collect and annotate a dataset and understand it in depth, and choose how to measure success and which validation metrics to monitor.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Constraints identified here, such as encryption or latency, later decide the deployment target, and the chosen metric guides all development.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Mistakes at this stage, such as unrepresentative data or the wrong metric, cannot be fixed by better modeling.

terminology.meaning: The metric (accuracy, ROC AUC, precision/recall, etc.) that defines what a good model is for this problem.

connections: p.202: understanding the data and choosing a measure of success

paragraphs.excerpt: Once you understand the problem and you have an appropriate dataset, develop
paragraphs.what_it_says: Phase 2: develop a model. Prepare the data; pick an evaluation protocol (hold-out or K-fold, and which portion to use for validation); beat a simple baseline to achieve statistical power; scale up to a model that can overfit; regularize and tune hyperparameters based on validation performance. Much ML research focuses only on this last step.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The order matters. First show that the signal is learnable (beat the baseline), then find enough capacity (overfit), then trade capacity for generalization (regularize and tune).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It gives a repeatable recipe for any new problem and stops you from regularizing a model that cannot yet learn.

terminology.meaning: Here: a model that beats a trivial baseline, showing that the inputs contain learnable signal.
Splitting data into K parts, training on K−1 and validating on the remaining one in turn, then averaging.

paragraphs.excerpt: When your model is ready and yields good performance on the test
paragraphs.what_it_says: Phase 3: deploy once test performance is good. Set appropriate expectations with stakeholders; optimize the final model for inference and ship it to the chosen environment (web server, mobile, browser, embedded device, etc.); monitor production performance and keep collecting data for the next generation.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Deployment covers communication, engineering and ongoing monitoring, and its last step feeds the next cycle.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It recaps section 6.3 and highlights that the last step loops back into data collection.

concepts.name: Universal workflow of machine learning
concepts.definition: The three-phase blueprint for any ML project: define the task, develop a model, deploy the model.
concepts.intuition: A project lifecycle in which training is the middle third.
concepts.technical: Define: context, data, metrics. Develop: prep, evaluation protocol, baseline, overfit, regularize/tune. Deploy: expectations, optimized inference model, monitoring and data collection for the next generation.
concepts.significance: Places model development in its full context; the rest of the book zooms into the middle phase.
concepts.example: The spam filter: constraints (encryption) → data → metric → model → on-device deployment → user surveys → retraining.
concepts.misconception: That ML is mostly about choosing architectures.

concepts.name: Model maintenance
concepts.definition: Getting ready to train the next model generation as soon as the current one launches.
concepts.intuition: Planning the next edition of a book while the current one is on shelves.
concepts.technical: Watch production data for new features and label-set changes; keep collecting/annotating, focusing on hard samples.
concepts.example: Adding a new 'scam link' label when a new kind of spam appears.
concepts.misconception: That maintenance means only retraining on new data. Features and labels may change too.

concepts.name: Collecting hard samples
concepts.definition: Prioritizing for annotation the samples the current model finds difficult to classify.
concepts.intuition: A student learns most from the problems they get wrong.
concepts.technical: The book says such samples are most likely to help improve performance; beyond the book, this is related to active learning and uncertainty sampling.
concepts.significance: Maximizes the value of each labeled sample.
concepts.example: Sending the cookie images with predicted probability near 0.5 to labelers.
concepts.misconception: That random new samples are as valuable as hard ones.

concepts.name: K-fold validation
concepts.definition: An evaluation protocol rotating K validation folds over the data.
concepts.intuition: Everyone takes a turn being the test audience.
concepts.technical: Listed in the summary alongside hold-out validation as a choice in the develop phase.
concepts.significance: Gives reliable estimates when data is scarce.
concepts.example: K = 4 on a small dataset: 4 trainings, average the 4 validation scores.
concepts.misconception: That it removes the need for a test set.

concepts.name: Overfitting (as a development milestone)
concepts.definition: Fitting the training data so closely that validation performance degrades.
concepts.intuition: Proof that the model has enough capacity, before reining it in.
concepts.technical: The workflow deliberately scales up until the model overfits, then regularizes and tunes.
concepts.significance: Shows where the capacity boundary is.
concepts.example: Adding layers until validation loss starts to rise after some epoch.
concepts.misconception: That overfitting should be avoided at every stage. In the workflow you aim for it first.

deeper.title: The workflow as a loop
deeper.body: The summary reads as a list, but its last item ("keep collecting data so you can develop the next generation") feeds back into phase 1's data collection and phase 2's development. Combined with concept drift (p.212), this means a production ML system goes through the define–develop–deploy cycle repeatedly. How often depends on the domain: days for fraud, weeks for music, years for image search. (Our synthesis.)

deeper.title: Picking hard samples in practice
deeper.body: Beyond the book, common ways to find samples that seem difficult: (1) **low confidence**, where the top predicted probability is near chance; (2) **disagreement** between an ensemble or between model generations; (3) **audit errors**, cases where the manual audit of p.212 found the model wrong; (4) **user reports**, e.g., spam users flag that got through. Route these to the annotation pipeline first.

deeper.title: Applying the summary to a new project
deeper.body: Example (ours): a plant-disease detector for farmers' phones. **Define**: farmers in fields with poor connectivity (constraint → on-device); collect photos from real fields, not lab images; metric: recall on diseased plants. **Develop**: resize images, use K-fold because data is scarce, beat the 'always healthy' baseline, scale up until it overfits, add augmentation and dropout. **Deploy**: explain the expected miss rate to agronomists, apply `model.quantize("int8")` and ship with TensorFlow Lite, survey farmers, and collect misclassified photos for the next generation.

misconceptions.claim: Once deployed, a model only needs retraining on fresh data of the same form.
misconceptions.correction: The book says to watch for new features and to consider expanding or editing the label set, so the problem definition itself can change.

misconceptions.claim: All new data is equally useful for the next model generation.
misconceptions.correction: Samples the current model finds difficult are the most likely to improve performance.

misconceptions.claim: Hyperparameter tuning is the core of an ML project.
misconceptions.correction: The authors note that much research focuses only on this step, but it is one part of a much larger workflow.
The summary orders the steps: beat a baseline, scale up until the model overfits, and only then regularize and tune.

takeaways: Start preparing the next model generation as soon as the current one launches.
Watch production data for new features and needed changes to the label set.
Keep collecting and annotating data, prioritizing samples the current model finds difficult.
The universal workflow has three phases: define the task, develop a model, deploy it.
Development order: prepare data, pick a protocol, beat a baseline, overfit, then regularize and tune.
Deployment: set expectations, optimize and ship, then monitor and keep collecting data.
Model development is only one part of the big picture.

questions.question: According to the book, which samples are most likely to help improve the next model generation?
options: Samples that seem difficult to classify for the current model
Samples the model classifies with very high confidence
Synthetic samples generated from the training set
questions.answer: Samples that seem difficult to classify for the current model
questions.explanation: The book says to pay special attention to hard samples because they are most likely to improve performance. Confidently classified samples add little new information, and random or synthetic samples are not what the page recommends.

questions.question: List the five steps of the 'develop a model' phase in order.
questions.answer: Prepare the data; pick an evaluation protocol; beat a simple baseline (achieve statistical power); scale up to a model that can overfit; regularize and tune hyperparameters on validation performance.
questions.explanation: Straight from the summary's second bullet.

questions.question: Why does the workflow ask you to build a model that overfits before regularizing?
questions.answer: Overfitting shows that the model has enough capacity to learn the training data. Only then is it meaningful to trade capacity for generalization through regularization and tuning; regularizing a model that underfits would make it worse.
questions.explanation: This is the ordering in the summary and section 6.2.4 (p.206).

questions.question: What two questions does the book suggest asking about production data when preparing the next generation?
questions.answer: Are new features becoming available? Should you expand or otherwise edit the label set?

questions.question: Which is the FIRST step of the deployment phase in the summary?
options: Collect data for the next generation
questions.explanation: The summary says 'First, make sure to set appropriate expectations with stakeholders.' Optimization, monitoring and data collection come after.

questions.question: In what sense is the universal workflow a loop rather than a straight line?
questions.answer: The final deployment step (monitor and keep collecting data) feeds the next generation's data collection and development. Concept drift guarantees that each model will eventually need replacing.
questions.explanation: This combines the maintenance bullets and the last summary item with p.212.

questions.question: Without looking, can you name the three steps of the 'define the problem' phase?
questions.answer: Understand the broader context (end goal and constraints); collect and annotate a dataset and understand it in depth; choose how to measure success and which validation metrics to monitor.
